Travel money field guide · 14 min read

One week in Japan can cost ¥76,000—or ¥1.1 million. The route is only half the answer.

Four travelers can take the same seven days, see Tokyo and Kyoto, and leave with radically different bills. Here is what each one actually sleeps in, eats, rides and does—and what those yen totals mean in dollars, euros, pounds and pesos.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published October 13, 2026 · Rates and operating details checked October 13

Ask what a week in Japan costs and you will often get a daily average. That answer is tidy and nearly useless. A hostel bed in Tokyo and a suite overlooking Kyoto are both “accommodation.” A bowl of gyūdon and a counter seat at a celebrated sushi restaurant are both “dinner.” A free morning at Meiji Jingu and a private guided excursion both occupy half a day.

So this guide starts with behavior, not a universal price. Each budget below is a model for one adult, seven days and six nights, priced in yen. It includes accommodation, food, travel inside Japan, admissions, activities and a modest contingency. It excludes the international flight, travel insurance and shopping because those three depend most heavily on origin, age, booking date and appetite.

The number that changes everything: moving between Tokyo and Kansai adds roughly a round-trip Shinkansen fare, but hotel category and dining choices create the much larger gap. The luxury traveler does not spend fourteen times more because the train goes fourteen times faster.

At a glance: four seven-day Japans

StyleRouteSleepWhat the week feels likeTotal
ShoestringTokyo + Yokohama/KamakuraHostel or capsule, 6 nightsFree neighborhoods, one day trip, casual food¥76,000
Comfortable classicTokyo → Kyoto → OsakaBusiness/mid-range hotelsShinkansen, temples, one special dinner¥198,000
Premium cultureTokyo → Hakone/Fuji → KyotoGood hotels + one ryokanOnsen, kaiseki, taxis when useful, guided culture¥473,000
LuxuryTokyo → Hakone → Kyoto/OsakaLuxury hotels and ryokanFine dining, private transfers and private guide¥1,103,000

1. The ¥76,000 week: stay in one region

Route: four full Tokyo days, one Kamakura or Yokohama day trip, and flexible arrival/departure days. Sleep in a well-reviewed hostel or capsule hotel near a useful railway line. Start with a bakery, supermarket or convenience-store breakfast; make lunch the larger restaurant meal; choose ramen, curry, soba, gyūdon or a set meal for dinner.

The experiences are real, not consolation prizes: Sensoji and the streets of Asakusa, Meiji Jingu, Shibuya after dark, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building view, Yanaka or Koenji, and a day by the sea in Kamakura. Pay for one museum, garden or observation deck rather than every famous rooftop.

¥30,0006 hostel/capsule nights
¥21,000food: ¥3,000 a day
¥8,000urban travel + day trip
¥6,000admissions and small experiences
¥3,000airport transfer allowance
¥8,000laundry, drinks and contingency

This plan works because it rejects the most expensive habit in a short trip: collecting distant cities. JNTO advises travelers with one week or less to consider one base and nearby day trips. Staying local saves both fares and the hours lost checking out, moving luggage and finding the next hotel.

2. The ¥198,000 classic: the route first-time visitors recognize

Route: three nights Tokyo, two nights Kyoto, one night Osaka; Shinkansen between Tokyo and Kyoto; departure from Kansai if an open-jaw international ticket makes sense. The days combine Shibuya and Meiji Jingu, Asakusa, a Kyoto temple-and-neighborhood day, Fushimi Inari early or late, Nara or Uji, and Osaka food streets.

This is the famous Golden Route compressed into one week. It is possible, but it is not relaxed. JNTO’s current guidance describes roughly ten days to two weeks as the more comfortable span for Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka. In seven days, every hotel change has to earn its place.

¥84,0006 rooms at an average ¥14,000
¥42,000food: ¥6,000 a day
¥31,000Shinkansen + local transport
¥18,000temples, museums and experiences
¥5,000airport connections
¥18,000coffee, luggage and contingency

The nationwide seven-day Japan Rail Pass is officially listed from ¥50,000. That does not automatically make it a bargain. A traveler taking one Tokyo–Kyoto journey and flying home from Osaka may spend less on individual tickets. Price the journeys you will actually take instead of treating the pass as a default.

3. The ¥473,000 week: buy time, food and one memorable night

Route: two nights Tokyo, one ryokan night in Hakone or the Fuji Five Lakes, three nights Kyoto. The traveler pays for comfort where it changes the experience: a room with space, a ryokan dinner and breakfast, reserved seats, luggage forwarding, occasional taxis, and one private or small-group cultural activity.

The itinerary does less than the classic route but goes deeper. Tokyo gets one neighborhood day and one food-and-museum day. The hot-spring night is treated as the destination, not a bed between trains. Kyoto gets an opening-time temple, a craft or tea experience, a slow Higashiyama walk and a Nara or Uji day.

¥240,000quality hotels + one ryokan package
¥100,000casual meals plus kaiseki/sushi
¥45,000rail, reserved seats and taxis
¥55,000guide, tea/craft and admissions
¥8,000airport and luggage services
¥25,000contingency

This is where “expensive” begins to mean access and time rather than gold fittings. Dinner is part of the ryokan stay. A taxi may prevent an hour of awkward transfers. A guide can make a garden or food district legible. The premium is worthwhile only if the traveler uses what it buys.

4. The ¥1,103,000 week: luxury is mostly space and people

Route: two luxury nights in Tokyo, a private-bath ryokan in Hakone, three luxury nights in Kyoto or Osaka. Add airport and intercity transfers where they genuinely reduce friction, a private guide for two days, hard-to-book dining, and a professionally led cultural experience.

The model assigns ¥600,000 to six nights, ¥210,000 to food, ¥120,000 to transport, ¥100,000 to guiding and experiences, and ¥73,000 to incidentals and contingency. A celebrated suite or top ryokan can push the total much higher; a traveler sharing rooms and transfers can bring the per-person figure down sharply.

The surprising part is what stays the same. Sensoji does not charge a luxury admission. Shibuya Crossing does not create a premium lane. Mount Fuji does not appear on command. Money can buy a better view from the room, a driver waiting below and a second morning near the mountain. It cannot purchase the weather or empty Kyoto’s streets.

What those yen totals mean at home

The conversion below uses European Central Bank reference rates dated October 12, 2026: €1 = ¥177.33, US$1.1181, £0.84478, A$1.6032, C$1.5946, NZ$1.9968, MX$20.5081 and ₱70.169. The Bank of Japan’s October 13 17:00 market range—about ¥158.21–¥158.22 per US dollar and ¥177.01–¥177.05 per euro—provides a same-day cross-check. Values are rounded and are comparisons, not card or cash quotes; banks add spreads and fees.

“Dollar” is not one currency, so the table separates US, Australian, Canadian and New Zealand dollars. “Peso” is not one currency either: Mexican and Philippine pesos are shown separately and must never be compared as if they were interchangeable. International airfare should be added in the currency in which you actually buy it.

Season can rewrite the hotel line

Cherry-blossom weeks, autumn foliage in Kyoto, Golden Week, Obon and the New Year period concentrate demand. Rooms can sell earlier, flexible rates disappear and the same category may cost far more than this model. There is no honest nationwide “sakura surcharge” percentage: bloom dates shift, cities peak at different times and hotel pricing is dynamic. For planning, build a 20–40% accommodation cushion during a must-see peak and replace it with live quotes before booking.

June’s rainy season and many weekdays in January or February can offer more availability, but the trade is weather, shorter daylight or seasonal closures. Summer can reduce room pressure in some cities while adding heat, humidity and festival spikes. Typhoon disruption is possible from summer into autumn. A cheap room is not a saving if the climate makes the itinerary miserable for you.

For Mount Fuji, season changes the activity entirely. Viewing is possible year-round when weather cooperates; climbing is limited to officially opened trails and dates. A Fuji day trip should never be priced as a guaranteed view. An overnight buys time, not certainty.

Couples, families and the cost per person

Solo travelers pay the full room alone. Two adults sharing a ¥20,000 room spend ¥10,000 each before local accommodation taxes, while hostel beds are normally priced per person. This is why the comfortable and luxury models may fall substantially per traveler for a couple, even though food, rail and admissions still multiply.

Families gain from shared rooms but face occupancy limits: Japanese hotel rooms can be compact, and a child’s age affects rail, meal and bedding rules. A family should price the actual room configuration, not double the solo budget or assume two children fit free. Apartment-style accommodation can reduce breakfast and laundry costs; luggage and taxi capacity can work the other way.

Japan’s international tourist tax rose to ¥3,000 on July 1, 2026 and is generally collected through the departure ticket. Check whether it is already included before adding it again. Local accommodation taxes in cities such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka vary by room price and jurisdiction and may be collected separately.

The best one-week budget is a decision about attention

The ¥76,000 traveler sees less geography and may experience more unplanned Tokyo. The ¥198,000 traveler buys the first-time route and accepts the pace. The ¥473,000 traveler converts money into a slower ryokan night, context and comfort. The ¥1.1 million traveler buys privacy, space and people’s time—but still shares the temple, weather and street with everyone else.

Begin with the experience you refuse to miss, then protect it. If that is food, stay in simpler rooms. If it is a ryokan, make the surrounding day quiet enough to enjoy it. If it is Tokyo street life, do not pay to spend half the week on trains. Watch Japan LIVE with Yuji before choosing a neighborhood; the distance between the famous sight and the ordinary street is where a realistic plan begins. And when menus, station signs and greetings become part of the trip, DraMap is Yuji’s iOS game for learning Japanese while playing.

A Japan budget is not a verdict on what the country costs. It is a map of what you chose to notice.
